note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

precepts.why:
At “the time when kings go forth to battle”, David sent Joab out against the children of Ammon, “But David tarried still at Jerusalem.” From the roof he saw Bath-sheba, sent and took her, and when she was with child, “David sent to Joab, saying, Send me Uriah the Hittite. And Joab sent Uriah to David.”

Joab was David’s nephew and the go between in the matter of Bathsheba and the killing of Uriah. Joab knew David’s dirt, which is why he often defied the king’s orders.

And here he defied them. The man who saw Absalom hanged in an oak would not touch him for a thousand shekels, “for in our hearing the king charged thee and Abishai and Ittai, saying, Beware that none touch the young man Absalom.” Joab said, “I may not tarry thus with thee”, took three darts, “and thrust them through the heart of Absalom, while he was yet alive in the midst of the oak.”

Joab was an evil man with the spirit of murder. He could have brought Absalom back alive for his father to make amends, but he did what he wanted. Ten young men that bare Joab’s armour compassed about and smote Absalom and slew him, for a beast will consort to his own like.

points: David numbered the people and set captains of thousands and hundreds, sending a third part under Joab, a third under Abishai, and a third under Ittai the Gittite. He said he would surely go forth with them himself.

note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

points: The people answered that he should not go, for he was worth ten thousand of them and it was better that he support them out of the city. David hearkened to their counsel and said what seemed best to them he would do; he did not run a dictatorship. In a time when he could not trust his own flesh and blood, he trusted the proven men he had warred with for years.

note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

points: David charged Joab, Abishai, and Ittai to deal gently for his sake with the young man, even with Absalom, and all the people heard the charge. Even after Absalom defiled his concubines and stole the people's hearts, David still sought to make amends with his son.

note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

points: The battle was in the wood of Ephraim, and Israel was slain before the servants of David in a great slaughter of twenty thousand men. The wood devoured more people that day than the sword devoured.

note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

points: Absalom, riding on a mule, went under the thick boughs of a great oak, and his head caught hold of the oak so that he was taken up between the heaven and the earth while the mule went on. He hung there yet alive.

note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

points: A man told Joab he had seen Absalom hanged in an oak. Joab asked why he had not smitten him to the ground for a reward of ten shekels and a girdle, but the man refused, saying he would not put forth his hand against the king's son for a thousand shekels, because he had heard the king charge them to beware that none touch the young man.

note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

points: The man told Joab that to have killed Absalom would have been to work falsehood against his own life, for nothing is hid from the king, and Joab himself would have set himself against him. Joab said he would not tarry, took three darts, and thrust them through the heart of Absalom while he was yet alive in the midst of the oak.

note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

points: Joab was an evil man with the spirit of murder; he could have brought Absalom back alive for his father to make amends, but he did what he wanted. Ten young men that bore Joab's armor compassed Absalom and smote him and slew him, for a beast will consort to his own like.

note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

points: Joab blew the trumpet and held back the people from pursuing Israel. They took Absalom, cast him into a great pit in the woods, and laid a very great heap of stones upon him, and all Israel fled everyone to his tent.

note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

points: In his lifetime Absalom had reared up a pillar for himself in the king's dale, saying he had no son to keep his name in remembrance, and he called it after his own name; it is called Absalom's place unto this day.

note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

points: Ahimaaz wanted to run and bear the king the tidings that the Lord had avenged him of his enemies, but Joab first sent Cushi, since the king's son was dead and this was not good news to carry. Ahimaaz pressed again and was allowed to run, and he outran Cushi by way of the plain.

note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

points: David sat between the two gates while the watchman on the wall saw first Ahimaaz running alone, then another man. The king said a man running alone brings tidings, and he recognized the running of Ahimaaz as a good man coming with good news.

note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

points: Ahimaaz fell before the king and said all was well, blessing the Lord who had delivered up the men that lifted their hand against the king; the good news was that David was alive and had overcome. When David asked if the young man Absalom was safe, Ahimaaz said he saw a great tumult but knew not what it was.

note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

points: Cushi came and said the enemies of the king and all that rose against him should be as that young man is. David understood that his son was one of the casualties of war. He was much moved, went up to the chamber over the gate, and wept, crying, O my son Absalom, would God I had died for thee. David's whole life was war, slaughtering giants from his youth up, and now he mourned in heartache for his son.
